cards.front: In Claude Code's explore, plan, and code loop, what must happen before the agent is allowed to move into the code phase and start writing changes?
cards.back: You must review and approve the plan (a structured description of the intended edits) that Claude Code produces after its exploration phase. Only after that approval does it move into the code phase.
cards.extra: M3 · Permission Modes & Human Gates · Claude Code agent loop, permission modes, settings, and where a human gate goes

cards.front: Independent of the permission system, why does Claude Code's explore-before-code sequence produce better output?
cards.back: Because Claude Code understands the codebase before touching anything, so it makes fewer assumptions and catches more downstream effects.
cards.extra: M3 · Permission Modes & Human Gates · Claude Code agent loop, permission modes, settings, and where a human gate goes

cards.front: Which Claude Code permission mode is the useful default for an unfamiliar codebase or high-stakes work, and what does it actually do?
cards.back: plan mode — it holds Claude Code in the explore phase, blocking all file edits and shell commands until you review and release the plan, so you can catch problems before anything is touched.
cards.extra: M3 · Permission Modes & Human Gates · Claude Code agent loop, permission modes, settings, and where a human gate goes

cards.front: In acceptEdits mode, which shell commands get auto-approved without a prompt, and what's the scope restriction on that auto-approval?
cards.back: Common filesystem commands (mkdir, touch, rm, rmdir, mv, cp, and sed) are auto-approved — but only for paths inside the working directory. All other shell commands, writes outside the working directory, and writes to protected paths still require confirmation.
cards.extra: M3 · Permission Modes & Human Gates · Claude Code agent loop, permission modes, settings, and where a human gate goes

cards.cloze_text: In Claude Code's auto permission mode, a classifier reviews each action, but even with everything otherwise auto-approved, {{c1::production deploys and migrations}}, {{c2::mass deletes}}, {{c3::credential exfiltration}}, and {{c4::force-push to main}} are blocked by default.
cards.extra: M3 · Permission Modes & Human Gates · Claude Code agent loop, permission modes, settings, and where a human gate goes

cards.front: What happens to a tool call in dontAsk mode that isn't on the pre-approved allow list and isn't a read-only command, and what is dontAsk actually built for?
cards.back: It's automatically denied — there's no confirmation queue to fall back to. dontAsk is built for locked-down CI pipelines and scripts, not for reducing friction on local interactive work.
cards.extra: M3 · Permission Modes & Human Gates · Claude Code agent loop, permission modes, settings, and where a human gate goes

cards.front: In bypassPermissions mode, which two commands are the sole exception that still triggers a prompt, and where is this mode appropriate to use?
cards.back: rm -rf / and rm -rf ~, as a last resort. Everything else runs with no confirmation and no safety checks, which is why this mode belongs only inside an isolated, disposable container or VM — never on a developer workstation against a live codebase.
cards.extra: M3 · Permission Modes & Human Gates · Claude Code agent loop, permission modes, settings, and where a human gate goes

cards.front: What's the difference between .claude/settings.json and .claude/settings.local.json in a Claude Code project?
cards.back: .claude/settings.json is committed to the repo and applies to everyone who clones it (team-wide conventions and allow/deny rules). .claude/settings.local.json is automatically git-ignored and holds personal overrides for just you on that one project.
cards.extra: M3 · Permission Modes & Human Gates · Claude Code agent loop, permission modes, settings, and where a human gate goes

cards.front: Why is an enterprise-level deny rule (managed-settings.json) described as the most durable governance control in Claude Code?
cards.back: It cannot be overridden or removed by any individual developer or project-level file, and it still applies even when a user has bypassPermissions set — a deny rule always wins over an allow rule regardless of mode.
cards.extra: M3 · Permission Modes & Human Gates · Claude Code agent loop, permission modes, settings, and where a human gate goes

cards.front: What single question should determine whether an agent's action needs a human approval gate before it runs?
cards.back: What is the worst outcome if this action runs without a person checking it? Low-cost, easily reversible actions can run without a gate; costly, hard-to-undo, or sensitive-path actions need one before they execute.
cards.extra: M3 · Permission Modes & Human Gates · Claude Code agent loop, permission modes, settings, and where a human gate goes

cards.front: For a change to code your team has marked sensitive, what role does the agent's own review play in the merge decision, and who must still act as the gate?
cards.back: The agent's work is only an input to the decision, not a replacement for one — a person must review and approve the change before it merges, no matter how confident the agent or its own review sounds.
cards.extra: M3 · Permission Modes & Human Gates · Claude Code agent loop, permission modes, settings, and where a human gate goes

cards.front: A developer's cleanup task ran under bypassPermissions and used a broad file pattern that matched both the intended /src/ directory and a production config directory, deleting files in both. What specific gate would have caught this before the deletion happened, and why did bypassPermissions remove it?
cards.back: The confirmation prompt on the script invocation itself (running cleanup.sh) — in default or acceptEdits mode, that script call would have required approval, giving the developer a chance to notice the pattern matched files outside /src/. bypassPermissions silences all confirmation prompts, including that one.
cards.extra: M3 · Permission Modes & Human Gates · The bypass mode that removed the one prompt that mattered

cards.front: If Claude Code had issued file deletions as direct rm commands on paths inside the working directory (instead of via a script), would default mode or acceptEdits mode still have prompted for confirmation?
cards.back: default mode would still prompt before the rm command runs. acceptEdits auto-approves common filesystem commands, including rm, on paths inside the working directory, so it would have let the deletion through silently.
cards.extra: M3 · Permission Modes & Human Gates · The bypass mode that removed the one prompt that mattered

cards.front: Besides silencing all confirmation prompts, what additional safety mechanism does bypassPermissions remove that default, acceptEdits, and plan mode all keep?
cards.back: The protected-path guard — so under bypassPermissions, even repo state and Claude's own configuration files lose their automatic prompt.
cards.extra: M3 · Permission Modes & Human Gates · The bypass mode that removed the one prompt that mattered

cards.front: What two mitigations does this lesson recommend if you want fewer permission prompts without losing the safety net that a full bypass mode removes?
cards.back: Set a deny rule on sensitive directories before switching modes, and prefer a classifier-gated mode like auto over a full bypass mode.
cards.extra: M3 · Permission Modes & Human Gates · The bypass mode that removed the one prompt that mattered

cards.front: Given a Claude Code setup that already auto-approves file edits for a trusted local refactor, what two settings.json rules do you add to (a) block destructive shell commands while still allowing safe ones, and (b) guarantee one specific file is never read?
cards.back: An allow/deny pair on Bash commands — e.g. allow Bash(npm run:*), deny Bash(rm:*) and Bash(git push:*) — plus a deny rule on Read(.env.production). The deny rule holds at the settings layer regardless of what the agent is asked to do during the session.
cards.extra: M3 · Permission Modes & Human Gates · Checkpoint 1: assemble the settings file and place the human gate

cards.front: For a trusted local refactor where destructive shell commands must be blocked, why does this lesson prefer an explicit deny rule over relying on auto mode's built-in safety classifier?
cards.back: The scenario calls for deterministic, predictable shell-gating. A classifier would likely also catch a destructive command, but an explicit deny rule doesn't depend on a classifier's judgment — it's guaranteed.
cards.extra: M3 · Permission Modes & Human Gates · Checkpoint 1: assemble the settings file and place the human gate

cards.front: Your settings auto-approve file edits for a refactor, but the agent proposes a change to a deployment configuration file that several production services read. Where should the human gate sit for that one action, and why?
cards.back: A human reviews and approves the change before the write executes — even though edits are auto-approved generally, this one write is hard to undo and reaches systems outside the file itself, so it crosses the worst-case-cost threshold that calls for a gate.
cards.extra: M3 · Permission Modes & Human Gates · Checkpoint 1: assemble the settings file and place the human gate

cards.front: When does the content of CLAUDE.md actually enter a Claude Code session, relative to your first message?
cards.back: It's read at the start of every session and appended to the prompt before any message from you arrives — so every convention in it is present from your very first prompt, without you having to restate it.
cards.extra: M3 · Durable Project Context · Durable project context with CLAUDE.md, rules files, hooks, and subagents

cards.front: What's the main failure mode of a growing CLAUDE.md file, and what's the actual mechanism behind it?
cards.back: Size dilution — a larger file consumes more of the context window, making any single instruction a smaller fraction of what loads, which reduces the chance the agent follows the one rule that catches a real mistake.
cards.extra: M3 · Durable Project Context · Durable project context with CLAUDE.md, rules files, hooks, and subagents

cards.front: What actually determines whether a rules file in .claude/rules/ is scoped to specific paths or loads unconditionally into every session — the YAML frontmatter, or which subdirectory it's placed in?
cards.back: The `paths` glob in its YAML frontmatter, not the subdirectory it's placed in. Subdirectories under .claude/rules/ are purely organizational — a rules file with no `paths` field loads unconditionally at launch, at the same priority as CLAUDE.md, no matter where it sits.
cards.extra: M3 · Durable Project Context · Durable project context with CLAUDE.md, rules files, hooks, and subagents

cards.front: Give the rule of thumb this lesson uses for deciding whether a constraint belongs in CLAUDE.md or in a scoped rules file.
cards.back: A constraint that applies everywhere in the project (e.g. 'never modify the database schema') belongs in CLAUDE.md. A constraint that only matters in one part of the codebase (e.g. 'all SQL in the database module must include an explicit transaction boundary') belongs in a rules file scoped with a `paths` glob to that area.
cards.extra: M3 · Durable Project Context · Durable project context with CLAUDE.md, rules files, hooks, and subagents

cards.front: You write a CLAUDE.md instruction telling the agent to run Prettier after every edit. What's the actual difference between that instruction and a PostToolUse hook that does the same thing?
cards.back: The CLAUDE.md instruction is followed most of the time, since it depends on the model choosing to comply. The hook fires independently of what the model decides — it runs every single time, with no exceptions.
cards.extra: M3 · Durable Project Context · Durable project context with CLAUDE.md, rules files, hooks, and subagents

cards.cloze_text: The core Claude Code hook lifecycle events are {{c1::PreToolUse}}, {{c2::PostToolUse}}, {{c3::UserPromptSubmit}}, {{c4::Stop}}, {{c5::Notification}}, {{c6::SessionStart}}, and {{c7::SessionEnd}}.
cards.extra: M3 · Durable Project Context · Durable project context with CLAUDE.md, rules files, hooks, and subagents

cards.front: Which Claude Code hook lifecycle event can actually block a tool call from executing, and what does the hook need to do to block it?
cards.back: PreToolUse — because it runs before the tool call executes, it can inspect the call and exit with code 2 to block it; whatever it writes to stderr becomes the feedback message the agent sees.
cards.extra: M3 · Durable Project Context · Durable project context with CLAUDE.md, rules files, hooks, and subagents

cards.front: Why can't a PostToolUse hook prevent a tool call it doesn't like, and what is it used for instead?
cards.back: PostToolUse runs after the tool call has already completed, so it cannot block it. It's used for side effects instead: running a formatter after an edit, triggering tests after a file change, or logging the operation for an audit trail.
cards.extra: M3 · Durable Project Context · Durable project context with CLAUDE.md, rules files, hooks, and subagents

cards.front: What two conditions cause Claude Code to fire a Notification hook event?
cards.back: When Claude needs permission to use a tool, or after Claude Code has been idle for 60 seconds.
cards.extra: M3 · Durable Project Context · Durable project context with CLAUDE.md, rules files, hooks, and subagents

cards.front: Which two built-in Claude Code subagents skip loading CLAUDE.md and git status, and why does that matter?
cards.back: Explore and Plan — they're optimized for speed. It matters because any project-level rule or repo state defined in CLAUDE.md won't be in their context when they run, so a CLAUDE.md rule you expect to apply may simply not be loaded.
cards.extra: M3 · Durable Project Context · Durable project context with CLAUDE.md, rules files, hooks, and subagents

cards.front: If a delegated task must respect your project's CLAUDE.md rules, which subagent should you use instead of Explore or Plan?
cards.back: The general-purpose subagent (or a custom subagent that explicitly loads the rules it needs) — general-purpose loads both CLAUDE.md and git status, unlike Explore and Plan.
cards.extra: M3 · Durable Project Context · Durable project context with CLAUDE.md, rules files, hooks, and subagents

cards.front: How does a custom subagent (defined in .claude/agents) actually gain access to a specific skill it needs?
cards.back: You must explicitly list that skill in the custom subagent's frontmatter — subagents don't automatically see your skills, and built-in agents have no preloaded skills at all.
cards.extra: M3 · Durable Project Context · Durable project context with CLAUDE.md, rules files, hooks, and subagents

cards.front: A CLAUDE.md file had grown to 847 lines and contained a correct rule ('do not modify /legacy/tokens/'), yet the agent still edited a file in that directory. Given the rule was present and the agent had access to it, what was the actual failure mode?
cards.back: Dilution — 846 other lines reduced the effective weight of the one instruction that mattered, not the agent lacking access to the rule.
cards.extra: M3 · Durable Project Context · The CLAUDE.md that kept growing until the rules stopped landing

cards.front: Per this lesson's fix for CLAUDE.md dilution, where should a historical decisions log or archived notes live instead of CLAUDE.md?
cards.back: In a separate reference document that the agent reads on demand — CLAUDE.md should stay a working set of rules that change current-session behavior, not a growing append log.
cards.extra: M3 · Durable Project Context · The CLAUDE.md that kept growing until the rules stopped landing

cards.front: This lesson says path-specific rules should move out of a bloated CLAUDE.md into rules files. What does it say about the one rule you truly cannot afford to have diluted?
cards.back: It should take the shortest path to becoming a hook — a hook enforces deterministically regardless of file size, instead of depending on the model noticing it among hundreds of other lines.
cards.extra: M3 · Durable Project Context · The CLAUDE.md that kept growing until the rules stopped landing

cards.front: You're writing a hook to block reads of .env.production. Which lifecycle event must the hook bind to in order to actually prevent the read, and why won't PostToolUse work for this?
cards.back: PreToolUse — it fires before the tool call executes, which is the only point at which blocking is possible. PostToolUse fires after the read has already happened, so it can only observe, not prevent it.
cards.extra: M3 · Durable Project Context · Checkpoint 2: select the correct value

cards.front: What must a PreToolUse hook's command actually do, beyond just detecting a protected file path, to make Claude Code treat the call as blocked?
cards.back: Exit with code 2 (after reading the tool call from stdin and checking the file path); anything written to stderr becomes the message Claude sees. A script that only logs or warns and exits 0 lets the call through regardless.
cards.extra: M3 · Durable Project Context · Checkpoint 2: select the correct value

cards.front: The same SKILL.md file can run in Claude Code, the Messages API, and the Agent SDK. What actually changes across these three runtimes — the file itself, or something else?
cards.back: Not the file itself. What changes is where the skill runs, how it gets loaded, and what it's allowed to touch.
cards.extra: M3 · Packaging Workflows · Packaging a workflow as a plugin: skills, custom commands, and marketplace install

cards.front: When a skill runs via the Messages API instead of Claude Code, where does it actually execute, and what does that mean for a skill that shells out to a local command?
cards.back: It executes inside Anthropic's code execution container, not your application's environment — so a skill that depends on a local command available in Claude Code will break on the Messages API, since that container doesn't have it.
cards.extra: M3 · Packaging Workflows · Packaging a workflow as a plugin: skills, custom commands, and marketplace install

cards.front: A skill that worked fine in Claude Code does nothing when run under the Agent SDK. What's the most common cause, and what configuration fixes it?
cards.back: settingSources (TypeScript) / setting_sources (Python) was never set, so filesystem sources like CLAUDE.md and skills never loaded. You must set it explicitly to the sources you intend — never rely on a default.
cards.extra: M3 · Packaging Workflows · Packaging a workflow as a plugin: skills, custom commands, and marketplace install

cards.front: Under Claude Managed Agents, when are skills attached to the agent, and how do you change which ones are available?
cards.back: Skills are attached when you define the agent as an API resource, not at session time — to change which skills are available, you update the agent definition itself.
cards.extra: M3 · Packaging Workflows · Packaging a workflow as a plugin: skills, custom commands, and marketplace install

cards.front: Why are Claude Managed Agents currently not eligible for Zero Data Retention or HIPAA BAA coverage?
cards.back: Because Managed Agents sessions run and are stored server-side, inside a sandbox Anthropic provisions and runs, rather than in your own environment.
cards.extra: M3 · Packaging Workflows · Packaging a workflow as a plugin: skills, custom commands, and marketplace install

cards.front: What's the one property a skill's description must have for the skill to load correctly in any runtime?
cards.back: It must clearly identify when the skill applies — the model loads a skill by matching your request against its description, so a vague description fails to load in every runtime, not just one.
cards.extra: M3 · Packaging Workflows · Packaging a workflow as a plugin: skills, custom commands, and marketplace install

cards.front: Skills have replaced an older mechanism for giving a workflow an explicit, named invocation. What was that older mechanism, and what frontmatter flag makes a skill run only on explicit invocation, never automatically?
cards.back: The older mechanism is the .claude/commands/ directory (still works, but now a legacy process). Add disable-model-invocation: true to a skill's frontmatter to make it explicit-invocation-only.
cards.extra: M3 · Packaging Workflows · Packaging a workflow as a plugin: skills, custom commands, and marketplace install

cards.front: A plugin named 'payments' ships a command called run-tests. What do you actually type to invoke it, and why does this let two different plugins ship a command with the same name?
cards.back: /payments:run-tests — plugin commands are automatically namespaced with the plugin's name as a prefix, so two plugins can each ship a run-tests command without colliding. Renaming the plugin renames all its commands.
cards.extra: M3 · Packaging Workflows · Packaging a workflow as a plugin: skills, custom commands, and marketplace install

cards.front: An admin sets a managed marketplace allowlist so users can only add approved marketplace sources. What additional managed setting is needed to actually push a marketplace to all users without each one running the add command themselves?
cards.back: extraKnownMarketplaces, paired with the allowlist — the allowlist alone only restricts what users can add, it doesn't register a marketplace for them automatically.
cards.extra: M3 · Packaging Workflows · Packaging a workflow as a plugin: skills, custom commands, and marketplace install

cards.front: If a plugin author's skill depended on a deny rule or hook they had configured locally on their own machine, does installing that plugin carry that protection over to a teammate's machine?
cards.back: Only if the deny rule or hook is explicitly included as part of the plugin bundle. A guardrail the author merely had configured locally is not carried over automatically — without it, the protection does not transfer with the install.
cards.extra: M3 · Packaging Workflows · Packaging a workflow as a plugin: skills, custom commands, and marketplace install

cards.front: A team wants the same review-checklist skill to run in two situations: (1) a developer typing in the Claude Code terminal, and (2) a backend service calling the Messages API directly. What configuration does each situation need?
cards.back: (1) Terminal: place SKILL.md in .claude/skills with a description matching review requests — Claude Code discovers it from the filesystem. (2) Messages API: send the code-execution and skills beta headers, and write the skill so it doesn't depend on local files or tools, since it runs inside Anthropic's execution container, not your service's environment.
cards.extra: M3 · Packaging Workflows · Checkpoint 3: place the skill in the right runtime

cards.front: A scheduled headless job built on the Agent SDK is supposed to pick up a skill from the repo, but it isn't loading. What's the fix, and why shouldn't you just assume it will work by default?
cards.back: Explicitly set settingSources (TypeScript) / setting_sources (Python) to include filesystem sources — whether the SDK loads CLAUDE.md and skills from the project is controlled by that setting, and you should never rely on its default behavior; confirm current default behavior against the reference at build time.
cards.extra: M3 · Packaging Workflows · Checkpoint 3: place the skill in the right runtime

cards.front: A product team wants a review-checklist skill to run inside a long-running agent that Anthropic hosts and that's reachable by an agent ID across sessions, rather than something the team runs itself. What's the right way to attach the skill, and where does it actually execute?
cards.back: Define the agent as an API resource that lists the skill (Claude Managed Agents), sending the managed-agents-2026-04-01 beta header. It executes inside a sandbox Anthropic provisions and runs, not your environment, so the skill's steps must not depend on local files.
cards.extra: M3 · Packaging Workflows · Checkpoint 3: place the skill in the right runtime

cards.front: A plugin installs successfully on every teammate's machine, but its skill only fails when they actually run it. What key distinction does this lesson draw between 'install' and 'execution' that explains why install success doesn't guarantee it will run?
cards.back: Install just copies files into place; execution resolves the paths and variables those files point at, against the machine actually running them. A plugin author's own machine-specific paths install fine everywhere but only resolve correctly on the author's own machine.
cards.extra: M3 · Packaging Workflows · The plugin that installed on your machine and failed on everyone else's

cards.front: What's the difference between $CLAUDE_PROJECT_DIR and ${CLAUDE_PLUGIN_ROOT}, and when do you use each in a skill or hook command?
cards.back: $CLAUDE_PROJECT_DIR references scripts stored in the project itself; ${CLAUDE_PLUGIN_ROOT} references scripts bundled inside the plugin. Use whichever matches where the script actually lives, so the path resolves correctly regardless of whose machine runs it or what directory the session started in.
cards.extra: M3 · Packaging Workflows · The plugin that installed on your machine and failed on everyone else's

cards.front: In the plugin failure story, why did the undocumented DEPLOY_TOKEN environment variable dependency cost three teammates two hours to debug, when the absolute-path bug was found quickly?
cards.back: The absolute path sat in plain text in SKILL.md, visible to a reviewer reading the file. The environment variable dependency wasn't documented anywhere in the plugin, so the skill ran fine right up until the step that needed it — only failing at that point, with nothing announcing the missing dependency.
cards.extra: M3 · Packaging Workflows · The plugin that installed on your machine and failed on everyone else's

cards.front: Beyond fixing paths and documenting environment variables, what's the recommended final check before distributing a plugin to a team?
cards.back: Test the install on a clean machine before distribution — this catches issues that the author's own build machine may be hiding (like cached files, pre-set env vars, or pre-existing directories).
cards.extra: M3 · Packaging Workflows · The plugin that installed on your machine and failed on everyone else's

cards.front: A SKILL.md step calls an absolute path (/Users/alexmorgan/.../validate.sh) that only exists on the author's machine. Two tempting 'fixes' — a home-directory shortcut (~/projects/...) or another absolute path to a shared network drive — are both still wrong. Why?
cards.back: Both still depend on a specific machine's layout: a home-directory shortcut still assumes the project lives at that exact location relative to home, and a network-drive path assumes every teammate has that drive mounted at that path. Only a path built from CLAUDE_PROJECT_DIR resolves correctly regardless of where the project was cloned.
cards.extra: M3 · Packaging Workflows · Checkpoint 4: fix the broken plugin definition

cards.front: Before MCP, if three different applications needed access to the same external service, what did each one have to do — and what does MCP change about that?
cards.back: Each application had to maintain its own separate tool schema and implementation. MCP separates the tool definition from any one application into a standalone server process, so you build the capability once and every MCP client that connects gets access without re-implementing it.
cards.extra: M3 · MCP Servers · Building and configuring an MCP server: transport, scope, and the GitHub server

cards.front: Besides tools, what's the second thing an MCP server can expose called a 'resource', and when is it the right pattern to reach for?
cards.back: A resource is read-only data the server exposes for the client to fetch and place directly into context, rather than the model calling a tool to retrieve it. Reach for it when you want known data in context from the start of a turn, and pulling it in directly is cheaper and more predictable than a tool call.
cards.extra: M3 · MCP Servers · Building and configuring an MCP server: transport, scope, and the GitHub server

cards.front: When is an MCP prompt (a pre-written instruction template the server exposes) the right tool to reach for, rather than just letting the user phrase their own request?
cards.back: When specific wording matters enough that a carefully built instruction produces materially better results than what a typical user would type, and you want every client connecting to the server to get that same quality — the prompt is maintained once on the server and reused everywhere.
cards.extra: M3 · MCP Servers · Building and configuring an MCP server: transport, scope, and the GitHub server

cards.cloze_text: MCP transport is the communication channel between client and server: {{c1::stdio}} runs the server as a local subprocess on the same machine as the client; {{c2::HTTP}} is the recommended transport for any server that doesn't run locally; {{c3::SSE}} is an older transport that HTTP has superseded and is no longer recommended for new servers.
cards.extra: M3 · MCP Servers · Building and configuring an MCP server: transport, scope, and the GitHub server

cards.front: By default, how does Claude Code handle the tool definitions from a connected MCP server, given that loading them all upfront would occupy the context window?
cards.back: It defers them rather than loading them all upfront, using a search step to discover and load only the specific tools a task actually calls for — so only the tools actually used enter context.
cards.extra: M3 · MCP Servers · Building and configuring an MCP server: transport, scope, and the GitHub server

cards.front: What's the opt-in alternative to Claude Code's default deferred MCP tool-loading behavior, and under what condition does it still fall back to deferring?
cards.back: An opt-in mode that loads tool definitions upfront, as long as they fit within roughly 10 percent of the context window — it only defers (falls back to search-based discovery) when that limit is exceeded.
cards.extra: M3 · MCP Servers · Building and configuring an MCP server: transport, scope, and the GitHub server

cards.front: In prompt caching, what happens if a single character changes before the cache breakpoint, and what's the consequence?
cards.back: The entire cache for that stable prefix is invalidated — any change before the cache point forces a fresh write, so you pay the full write cost again instead of getting the cheaper cache-read cost.
cards.extra: M3 · MCP Servers · Building and configuring an MCP server: transport, scope, and the GitHub server

cards.front: How do you turn prompt caching on for a request in the Messages API, given there's no global caching setting?
cards.back: You mark a cache breakpoint by adding a cache_control field of type ephemeral to the last content block you want cached — this caches everything up to and including that block. You can place up to four breakpoints.
cards.extra: M3 · MCP Servers · Building and configuring an MCP server: transport, scope, and the GitHub server

cards.front: What are the two available cache lifetimes for prompt caching, and which workload pattern suits each?
cards.back: Five minutes (the default, resets on each read — suits frequent back-and-forth requests) and one hour (opt-in via a ttl of 1h on the breakpoint — suits workloads with longer gaps between requests, like an agent that pauses between steps, where the 5-minute window would expire before the next request).
cards.extra: M3 · MCP Servers · Building and configuring an MCP server: transport, scope, and the GitHub server

cards.front: What's the minimum token threshold below which prompt caching won't apply, even with a breakpoint set?
cards.back: 1,024 tokens for most current models — short prompts under that threshold will not be cached even if a breakpoint is set.
cards.extra: M3 · MCP Servers · Building and configuring an MCP server: transport, scope, and the GitHub server

cards.front: Both classical RAG and agentic search do the same fundamental thing. What's the core difference in timing between them?
cards.back: Both find a relevant slice of material and generate from it, but classical RAG finds that slice by matching against an index built in advance (chunks and embeddings prepared upfront); agentic search finds it by searching live, at the moment of need, with no pre-built index.
cards.extra: M3 · MCP Servers · Building and configuring an MCP server: transport, scope, and the GitHub server

cards.front: Why does retrieval (RAG) let a knowledge base grow to thousands of documents without each request getting more expensive?
cards.back: Because the model only ever receives the slice relevant to the current question, not the entire library — the cost of each request stays flat as the source material grows, since the request doesn't grow with it.
cards.extra: M3 · MCP Servers · Building and configuring an MCP server: transport, scope, and the GitHub server

cards.front: Why does file naming and organization matter for RAG quality, given that retrieval is 'only as good as what it finds'?
cards.back: The model can only reason over the slice retrieval hands it — if retrieval misses the document you needed because it's named vaguely (e.g. 'notes_final_v3.pdf') or ungrouped, the model never sees it, no matter how good the model is. Descriptive names and grouping related files improves what gets surfaced.
cards.extra: M3 · MCP Servers · Building and configuring an MCP server: transport, scope, and the GitHub server

cards.cloze_text: MCP server configuration scope determines which users and projects load the server: {{c1::Local}} scope stores the config in ~/.claude.json under the current project's path and isn't shared with teammates; {{c2::User}} scope stores it in your personal settings and applies across all your projects but stays personal; {{c3::Project}} scope writes it to a committed .mcp.json at the repo root so everyone who clones the repo gets it; {{c4::Enterprise}} scope deploys it through centrally managed, admin-controlled configuration.
cards.extra: M3 · MCP Servers · Building and configuring an MCP server: transport, scope, and the GitHub server

cards.front: A stdio MCP server is project-scoped and committed in .mcp.json so the whole team gets it. What does each teammate's machine still need for the server to actually run, and why?
cards.back: The runtime the launch command depends on (e.g. Node, if it's launched with npx) installed locally — because a stdio server spawns as a subprocess from each teammate's own machine; the committed config only stores the launch command, not the runtime itself.
cards.extra: M3 · MCP Servers · Building and configuring an MCP server: transport, scope, and the GitHub server

cards.front: How do you write a permission rule that targets one specific tool on an MCP server (say, GitHub's create_issue) rather than the whole server, and what happens to that server's other tools?
cards.back: Name it as mcp__server__tool, e.g. mcp__github__create_issue. An allow rule on that one tool lets it run without a prompt while every other tool on the same server still prompts; a deny rule on one tool blocks it while the server's other tools stay available. A deny on one tool overrides an allow on the whole server.
cards.extra: M3 · MCP Servers · Building and configuring an MCP server: transport, scope, and the GitHub server

cards.front: In the API MCP connector, what's the difference between the per-tool 'enabled' flag on an mcp_toolset object and a permission rule on an MCP tool?
cards.back: The enabled flag decides whether the model sees the tool at all (a context-cost and scope control); a permission rule decides whether a tool the model can see is actually allowed to run (a governance control). They're often used together.
cards.extra: M3 · MCP Servers · Building and configuring an MCP server: transport, scope, and the GitHub server

cards.front: The GitHub MCP server and the Linear MCP server are both remote HTTP servers using the same transport and scope logic. What's the one thing that differs between them, and how does each authenticate?
cards.back: Authentication. GitHub uses a Personal Access Token you generate and pass as a Bearer token via an environment variable reference. Linear uses OAuth — a browser-based sign-in flow where, after you approve access, a token is issued and stored automatically with no credential handled by hand.
cards.extra: M3 · MCP Servers · Building and configuring an MCP server: transport, scope, and the GitHub server

cards.front: An API key committed inline in .mcp.json spread to a developer's machine, three teammates' machines, and a CI runner within 48 hours. Once discovered and rotated, what made the fix costly beyond just generating a new key?
cards.back: The same key had already been configured into two other external services, so rotating it broke those two services too — three hours of extra work, on top of updating .mcp.json to use an environment variable instead.
cards.extra: M3 · MCP Servers · The API key that traveled with the configuration file into the repository

cards.front: This lesson recommends two layers to stop an agent from writing credential values directly into a committed .mcp.json. What are they, and how do their roles differ?
cards.back: A CLAUDE.md convention instruction ('credential values must never be written inline to .mcp.json') signals the rule to the model each session; a PreToolUse hook that inspects write/edit operations against .mcp.json for credential-like patterns and exits with a blocking code enforces it deterministically regardless of what the model decides — the same hook-versus-instruction distinction as elsewhere in the module.
cards.extra: M3 · MCP Servers · The API key that traveled with the configuration file into the repository

cards.front: What's the correct long-term fix pattern for an API key that was mistakenly committed inline in an MCP server config, and why must the original key be treated as compromised even after the fix?
cards.back: Move the value to an environment variable and reference the variable in the configuration file (e.g. Bearer ${WAREHOUSE_MCP_TOKEN}). The original key must still be rotated, because it's already in repository history and cannot be cleaned out by a later commit that simply overwrites the file.
cards.extra: M3 · MCP Servers · The API key that traveled with the configuration file into the repository

cards.front: You're testing an experimental MCP server against one repository this week and aren't ready to share it with the team. What actually determines whether it stays private — the transport you pick, or the scope?
cards.back: Scope. Either stdio or HTTP works fine for an experiment like this — what keeps the configuration personal and out of version control is choosing local scope, not the choice of transport.
cards.extra: M3 · MCP Servers · Checkpoint 5: match transport and scope to each deployment scenario

cards.front: Two common mistakes when matching transport and scope to a deployment: using stdio for a company-hosted service, and using project scope for a personal experiment. Why does each one fail?
cards.back: stdio runs the server as a subprocess on your own machine, so it can't reach a service hosted on company infrastructure — that needs HTTP. Project scope commits the configuration to .mcp.json, which shares it with everyone who clones the repo — for an experiment you're not ready to share, that's the opposite of what you want; local scope is what keeps it personal.
cards.extra: M3 · MCP Servers · Checkpoint 5: match transport and scope to each deployment scenario

cards.cloze_text: A production enterprise integration, unlike a prototype that just confirms the connection works, must also answer: {{c1::who is the model acting as, and is that identity auditable}}, {{c2::what data can it access and where does that data leave the organization}}, {{c3::can an administrator lock the configuration so no individual developer can change it}}, and {{c4::can the access be logged in a way that satisfies a compliance audit}}.
cards.extra: M3 · Enterprise Integration · Connecting Claude to enterprise systems and authenticating it securely

cards.front: For a remote service tied to individual user identity, what does the MCP server send to signal that OAuth authentication is needed, and what happens next?
cards.back: The MCP server returns a 401 Unauthorized, which signals to the client that authentication is required; the client then initiates a browser-based sign-in flow, and after the user approves access, a token is issued and stored automatically with nothing copied by hand.
cards.extra: M3 · Enterprise Integration · Connecting Claude to enterprise systems and authenticating it securely

cards.front: For a CI pipeline running the Agent SDK that needs a service-identity API key, where should that key actually come from at runtime?
cards.back: Injected as a secret by the pipeline runner itself, not baked into the code — the key lives in the environment at the point of execution.
cards.extra: M3 · Enterprise Integration · Connecting Claude to enterprise systems and authenticating it securely

cards.front: For a local service reached over stdio transport with no network authentication, what actually serves as the security boundary, and what enforces it in practice?
cards.back: The file-system permission model itself is the security boundary — a deny rule in the settings files is the governance layer that enforces it.
cards.extra: M3 · Enterprise Integration · Connecting Claude to enterprise systems and authenticating it securely

cards.front: What's the core practice this lesson calls 'separation', and why does it matter mechanically, given what happens to configuration files over their lifetime?
cards.back: A credential never travels with the configuration that references it — the config file holds only a variable reference, and the value lives elsewhere. It matters because configuration files get committed, shared, and cloned; a value written inline rides along with every one of those copies, and once it enters a commit it stays in history in a way overwriting doesn't undo.
cards.extra: M3 · Enterprise Integration · Connecting Claude to enterprise systems and authenticating it securely

cards.front: When should you reach for a plain environment variable versus a managed secret store for holding a credential's actual value?
cards.back: An environment variable when the secret is local and short-lived (e.g. one machine or one CI pipeline run). A secret store when the secret is shared across several services or people — it centralizes the value so one rotation updates every consumer, and it records who read what for audit purposes.
cards.extra: M3 · Enterprise Integration · Connecting Claude to enterprise systems and authenticating it securely

cards.front: Why is rotation described as 'the only appropriate response to a leaked key', rather than just one option among several?
cards.back: Because a key that has been exposed cannot be made secret again — you must issue a new one. There's no way to un-leak a credential; replacing it is the only path back to a secure state.
cards.extra: M3 · Enterprise Integration · Connecting Claude to enterprise systems and authenticating it securely

cards.front: Why does a credential value baked into committed code resist clean rotation, compared to one read from an environment variable or secret store?
cards.back: The old value stays in commit history regardless of later edits, and every consumer hardcoded to that value breaks the moment it changes. A credential referenced by name from an environment variable or secret store rotates without touching the code that uses it, because the code references the name, and the name doesn't change when the value behind it does.
cards.extra: M3 · Enterprise Integration · Connecting Claude to enterprise systems and authenticating it securely

cards.front: What two habits does this lesson recommend to make credential rotation cheaper when it does happen?
cards.back: Scope each credential to the narrowest access its task needs (so a leak only reaches what that one integration required), and keep a record of which services use each credential (so a rotation doesn't have to first discover its own consumers).
cards.extra: M3 · Enterprise Integration · Connecting Claude to enterprise systems and authenticating it securely

cards.front: How does an audit hook (a PostToolUse hook logging every tool call and its parameters) answer a regulated customer's logging question, specifically regarding what the model can and can't do about it?
cards.back: It fires deterministically for every tool call regardless of what the model decides, so the log is not something the model can skip — giving compliance reviewers a record that doesn't depend on the model choosing to comply.
cards.extra: M3 · Enterprise Integration · Connecting Claude to enterprise systems and authenticating it securely

cards.front: What two things together give a compliance reviewer a checkable answer to 'where does our data get processed'?
cards.back: An MCP server configured with an HTTP endpoint in a specific region, combined with a platform deployment that pins processing to that same region.
cards.extra: M3 · Enterprise Integration · Connecting Claude to enterprise systems and authenticating it securely

cards.front: For a code modernization engagement on an unfamiliar legacy codebase, what specific risk does plan mode address, distinct from what hooks and CLAUDE.md each address?
cards.back: Plan mode holds the agent in the read-only explore phase, letting you review proposed edits and catch anything touching unexpected paths before a single file is modified — separate from hooks (which enforce guardrails against edits to specific paths during sensitive phases) and CLAUDE.md (which carries the new target-pattern conventions so the agent doesn't drift back to legacy patterns it reads in the surrounding code).
cards.extra: M3 · Enterprise Integration · Connecting Claude to enterprise systems and authenticating it securely

cards.cloze_text: Before starting high-risk agentic work like code modernization, this lesson says to answer three questions: {{c1::what is the blast radius if something goes wrong}}, {{c2::how are changes audited}}, and {{c3::who approves each phase before the next one begins}}.
cards.extra: M3 · Enterprise Integration · Connecting Claude to enterprise systems and authenticating it securely

cards.front: An OAuth-based MCP integration passed all staging tests, but every production sign-in attempt failed with a redirect URI mismatch. What was actually wrong, given the code itself had no defect?
cards.back: OAuth redirect URIs are registered per host, and the OAuth app registration only listed the staging host — the production host's URI was never added to the allowed list, so every sign-in attempt failed the URI match and looped back to the sign-in screen.
cards.extra: M3 · Enterprise Integration · The OAuth connection that worked in staging and failed in production

cards.front: Beyond just adding the production redirect URI, what additional requirement does this lesson flag for regulated enterprise customers regarding OAuth app registrations across environments?
cards.back: Most regulated enterprise customers require separate OAuth app registrations for each environment (staging and production) as a security policy — reusing the same app registration across environments is flagged as a second issue, not just the missing redirect URI.
cards.extra: M3 · Enterprise Integration · The OAuth connection that worked in staging and failed in production

cards.front: What's the practical takeaway for deployment checklists, given that an OAuth flow working end-to-end in staging says nothing about production readiness?
cards.back: Add the OAuth registration step (the new host's redirect URI, and possibly a separate app registration) explicitly to the deployment checklist — so it's caught before the first production sign-in attempt, not discovered by users hitting a redirect loop.
cards.extra: M3 · Enterprise Integration · The OAuth connection that worked in staging and failed in production

cards.front: A connection trace shows an MCP client getting a 401 Unauthorized both on the first attempt and after retrying with the same credential, which was read from a plaintext file. Why is 'just rotate the key' alone not a complete fix here?
cards.back: Rotating clears the 401 because a fresh key is one the service will accept, but if the new key gets written straight back into the same plaintext file at the same known path, the storage defect that caused the exposure is still in place — the next rotation just reproduces the same problem. The fix must both replace the rejected key and move it out of the file.
cards.extra: M3 · Enterprise Integration · Checkpoint 6: diagnose the authentication failure from a trace

cards.front: In that same scenario (a rejected key read from a plaintext credentials file), why is switching from API-key auth to OAuth not the right targeted fix?
cards.back: OAuth fits remote services tied to individual user identity. This is a service-account connection using a service credential, not a user sign-in, so OAuth doesn't match the identity model here — and switching auth mechanisms doesn't address what the trace actually shows, which is a rejected key stored insecurely.
cards.extra: M3 · Enterprise Integration · Checkpoint 6: diagnose the authentication failure from a trace

cards.front: A broken integration handoff is reviewed by checking three separate layers for planted defects. What are those three layers, drawing on this module's structure?
cards.back: The Claude Code configuration layer (settings.json permission modes and deny rules), the plugin or packaging layer (skill and command portability), and the MCP or authentication layer (server configuration and credential handling) — a realistic integration review has to check across all three, since a bug in one layer doesn't imply the others are clean.
cards.extra: M3 · Cumulative Integration Task · Cumulative integration task: checkpoint

cards.front: In the corrected settings.json for a production migration workstation, the fix sets defaultMode to acceptEdits rather than the more restrictive default mode. Why is acceptEdits the right tradeoff here, even though this is production work?
cards.back: acceptEdits auto-approves file edits and common filesystem commands while still gating destructive shell commands, which matches what this migration actually needs — the risk that mattered was bypassPermissions removing shell-command safety entirely, not the presence of edit-approval prompts. The right mode matches the task's actual risk profile rather than a blanket 'most restrictive is always safest' rule, and the .env.production deny rule stays in place regardless of mode.
cards.extra: M3 · Cumulative Integration Task · Cumulative integration task: assembly

cards.front: Per this module, what kind of AI code-review findings should you trust directly, versus what should you treat as needing separate verification?
cards.back: Trust findings the reviewer can prove from the diff in front of it, like a missing null check or an unclosed resource, and confirm them on the lines it cites. Treat any claim about runtime behavior or another system as a hypothesis to test, since the reviewer made that claim without the evidence that would prove it.
cards.extra: M3 · Key Takeaways · Seven key takeaways

cards.front: Per this module, where should the human review gate sit when using an AI code reviewer, and what's the other lever for improving the reviewer's own accuracy?
cards.back: Put the human gate at the point where a finding turns into an action that's hard to reverse. Separately, you raise the reviewer's accuracy by giving it the conventions it would otherwise have to guess at.
cards.extra: M3 · Key Takeaways · Seven key takeaways

cards.front: What is the Claude Agent SDK, in relation to what Claude Code runs in the terminal?
cards.back: A programmable interface that exposes the same agent loop Claude Code runs in the terminal — it lets developers invoke that loop from code, set the permission mode and available tools, and run tasks without an interactive session. The same permission model and deny rules that apply in the terminal also apply in the SDK.
cards.extra: M3 · Key Takeaways · Key terms from this module

cards.front: Roughly how many lines can a CLAUDE.md file grow to before it risks diluting its own critical rules, per this module's glossary?
cards.back: Roughly 200-300 lines — beyond that, content weight risks diluting the rules that matter most.
cards.extra: M3 · Key Takeaways · Key terms from this module
